analysis.one_liner: Repeals DC's Home Rule Act, ending the city's elected local government.
analysis.headline: The bill to strip Washington, DC of its elected local government never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would repeal the District of Columbia Home Rule Act, the law that lets DC residents elect a mayor and council to run their own city. Repeal would hand direct control of DC's laws, budget, and elections back to Congress. The bill was introduced by one House Republican with a handful of cosponsors and was never taken up by either committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of Congress would gain direct lawmaking power over the District of Columbia. DC's roughly 680,000 residents would lose their elected local government entirely; they would be governed by a Congress in which they have no voting representative.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Members of Congress, not DC residents

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the District of Columbia Home Rule Act, which is the charter that authorizes DC officials to legislate, conduct elections, and govern local affairs [S2] [S3].
The repeal is total and unconditional: the bill repeals the entire Home Rule Act with no transition plan, returning all local authority over the city to Congress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: DC residents would bear the entire cost. They would lose their elected mayor and council and be ruled directly by federal lawmakers they did not elect, with no vote in either chamber that would control their city.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire Home Rule Act at once with no transition provisions, which would leave open questions about the status of DC's budget, employees, contracts, and existing local laws [S3].

Under the Constitution, Congress already holds ultimate authority over the District, so repeal would not fix a gap in federal power; it would replace a locally elected government with direct control by a Congress in which DC residents have no voting member [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no mechanism, transition, or replacement government; its sole effect is to remove DC residents' elected local government and substitute rule by federal lawmakers they cannot vote for or against. Whatever oversight concerns supporters raise about DC governance already exist under the Home Rule Act, which gives Congress final authority over DC law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Oversight and Rules committees in August 2023 and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Andrew Ogles introduced the Seat of Government Act on August 11, 2023, to repeal the DC Home Rule Act [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability and, in addition, to the House Committee on Rules on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: DC residents and their elected local government, who kept self-rule because the bill never advanced. Its sponsors gained a stated position on the record without needing to build majority support for a measure that would have stripped 680,000 people of their local vote.

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Accountability
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 11, 2023 and took no action on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican: one sponsor and three cosponsors, all House Republicans, with no Democratic support and no floor action of any kind.

industries.note: Repeal would transfer full legislative authority over DC from an elected local government to Congress itself, consolidating power in incumbent federal officeholders who face no accountability from the people they would govern. The gain for Congress is the loss for DC residents.

industries.industry: DC local government and its elected officials
industries.note: The city's elected mayor, council, and local institutions would be abolished outright, eliminating the local democratic channel residents currently use to govern themselves.
